prompt: Use case: ui-mockup. Create one high-fidelity desktop web app lesson-player screen, landscape 16:10, edge-to-edge, crisp readable English UI, no device mockup or outer caption. This is a design proposal, not implementation. Product: HISTORY, an interactive history learning app. Same sample chapter in every alternative: The Silk Roads / At the crossroads, chapter 2 of 5. The attached reference contributes ONLY the Worlds identity: inky navy, rich plum, warm ivory, restrained amber controls, classical editorial lettering, luminous historical illustrations. Do not copy its three-phone layout or reuse its art as wallpaper. Preserve compact navigation: HISTORY, Chapters, bookmark, Sources, sound. Bottom controls: Previous, a five-part chapter progress indicator, Next. Narration is optional and user-paced: show Read / Listen, play/pause and seek; Next remains usable while audio plays. Visible prose must teach real history, not give instructions about the UI. No quiz, radio choices, scores, fake citations, generic card dashboard, oversized slogan, giant empty header, or essay hidden below the viewport. Generated historical imagery is visibly labeled Reconstruction; map routes schematic. Composition: a cinematic explorable reconstruction is the working surface itself. A newly composed cutaway caravanserai at Samarkand fills the central scene: courtyard, storerooms, shaded exchange arcade, loaded pack animals, distant road. Three discreet anchored inspectable labels name tangible places: “Courtyard”, “Storeroom”, “Exchange arcade”. The exchange arcade is selected, subtly illuminated; other areas remain quiet. A broad integrated plum reading ledge occupies the lower quarter, within the SAME viewport, with title “A city made exchange possible” and two readable paragraphs: “Long-distance trade rarely meant one merchant crossing Asia. Goods passed through overlapping regional networks, changing hands as people arranged transport, credit and a place to stay.” “In a city such as Samarkand, interpreters and trading communities helped merchants negotiate across languages. The city was an exchange of knowledge as well as goods.” A small inset situates Samarkand between broad east–west connections without competing with the scene. A slim scene rail shows Arrival / Exchange / Departure, selected Exchange, with Next passage. Include a modest “Why merchants stopped here” evidence link. Deeply composed museum-quality art and text, actual interface affordances, not a photograph with a headline.
purpose: Lesson-player composition proposal; illustrative artwork and unverified generated map/chronology labels.
approval: User 2026-11-22: likes all four, including spatial exploration; build a fluid system using these references.
